## The accessibility paradox

Scientific evaluation and public availability concern partly different product sets. The **mixed-diabetes (type 1 diabetes, T1D; and type 2 diabetes, T2D)** audit by [Reinders et al. (2024)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.diabres.2024.111833) reviewed 21 studies, 23 research-origin games and 13 app-store games. Their audit found:

1. **21 of 23 research-origin games were not publicly available.**
2. No identified web or personal-computer research game could be located.
3. Only one of 11 research mobile games was free in Google Play.
4. All 13 app-store games were visible in Apple’s store, five were visible in Google Play and 11 were free.
5. The public products generally lacked peer-reviewed product-level outcome evaluation.

The 21/23 figure describes non-availability/non-release at an audit, **not a longitudinal disappearance rate**. It does not establish that all games had previously been public, or why access was absent. This is not a quality ranking. Research prototypes can generate valuable design and feasibility evidence without becoming distributable products. Public products can be maintained and widely used without having undergone independent comparative evaluation. A useful knowledge base must therefore report **evidence** and **availability** as separate dimensions.

## Finding a usable product

Use the [catalogue's access filter](../../explorer.html) to distinguish public products, uncertain acquisition, study-only interventions, research prototypes and discontinued games. Each record gives its price, language, device requirements, account restrictions and verification date.

An official information page is not necessarily an acquisition route. For example, [Novi-Chek](../../explorer.html#game-novi-chek) retained a product page while its tested store links returned HTTP 404 in September 2026. [FlightGlucose](../../explorer.html#game-flightglucose) had indexed product information, but direct local connections failed. Those records remain uncertain rather than being counted as working public games.

“Free” describes price, not the absence of an account, data collection, a compatible device or regional restrictions. A study login or an obsolete executable is also different from a maintained public release.

## Why access may fail to become routine use

Adjacent sustainability reviews identify organisational, funding and technical barriers, but do not estimate their causal contribution to T1D-game non-availability ([Braithwaite et al., 2020](https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2019-036453); [Kaboré et al., 2022](https://doi.org/10.3389/fdgth.2022.1014375)). Relevant hypotheses include:

1. **No maintenance owner:** a study funds development and evaluation without funding app signing, hosting, updates and user support afterwards.
2. **An inaccessible dependency:** a game depends on specialist hardware, a discontinued service, a regional storefront or a study account.
3. **A mismatch with teaching needs:** an intervention designed for children, one procedure or a supervised study may not suit a newly diagnosed adult or a short clinical appointment.
4. **Unclear handover:** evidence, design rationale, translations and technical knowledge remain with individuals rather than in maintained project records.

These are system-level hypotheses, not explanations of any particular person's diagnosis education. The [sustainability chapters](../sustainability/why-games-disappear.qmd) examine the evidence and the [maintenance patterns](../sustainability/maintenance-patterns.qmd) translate it into proposed operational practices.
